questions.question: Suppose that [latex]L_1[/latex] is a regular language and [latex]L_2[/latex] is a context-free language. Which one of the following languages is NOT necessarily context-free?

options.A: [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex]
options.B: [latex]L_1\cdot L_2[/latex]
options.C: [latex]L_1 - L_2[/latex]
options.D: [latex]L_1\cup L_2[/latex]

questions.explanation:
With [latex]L_1[/latex] regular and [latex]L_2[/latex] CFL:
- [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex], [latex]L_1\cdot L_2[/latex], [latex]L_1\cup L_2[/latex] are always CFL (closure properties).
- [latex]L_1-L_2=L_1\cap\overline{L_2}[/latex] needs the complement of a CFL, which need not be CFL. E.g. [latex]L_1=\Sigma^*[/latex] gives just [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L_1-L_2[/latex]

questions.question: Let P be an array containing n integers. Let t be the lowest upper bound on the number of comparisons of the array elements, required to find the minimum and maximum values in an arbitrary array of n elements. Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: [latex]t \gt 2n-2[/latex]
options.B: [latex]t \gt 3\lceil \frac{n}{2}\rceil \text{ and } t\leq 2n-2[/latex]
options.C: [latex]t \gt n \text{ and } t\leq 3\lceil \frac{n}{2}\rceil[/latex]
options.D: [latex]t \gt \lceil \log_2(n)\rceil \text{ and } t\leq n[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Process elements in pairs: compare the two, then compare the smaller with the current min and the larger with the current max. That is 3 comparisons per 2 elements: about [latex]\lceil3n/2\rceil-2[/latex] comparisons, and this is optimal.

So [latex]t \gt n[/latex] and [latex]t\le3\lceil n/2\rceil[/latex].

Answer: [latex]t \gt n[/latex] and [latex]t\le3\lceil\frac n2\rceil[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
Consider the following three functions.

[latex]f_1=10^n\; f_2=n^{\log n}\;f_3=n^{\sqrt {n}}[/latex]

Which one of the following options arranges the functions in the increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?

options.A: [latex]f_3, f_2, f_1[/latex]
options.B: [latex]f_2, f_1, f_3[/latex]
options.C: [latex]f_1, f_2, f_3[/latex]
options.D: [latex]f_2, f_3, f_1[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Write each as a power of 2:
- [latex]f_2=n^{\log n}=2^{(\log n)^2}[/latex]
- [latex]f_3=n^{\sqrt n}=2^{\sqrt n\log n}[/latex]
- [latex]f_1=10^n=2^{n\log10}[/latex]

Compare exponents: [latex](\log n)^2 \lt \sqrt n\log n \lt n\log 10[/latex] for large n.

Answer: [latex]f_2,f_3,f_1[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.

S1: The sequence of procedure calls corresponds to a preorder traversal of the activation tree.
S2: The sequence of procedure returns corresponds to a postorder traversal of the activation tree.

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.B: S1 is false and S2 is true
options.C: S1 is true and S2 is true
options.D: S1 is false and S2 is false

questions.explanation:
In an activation tree a procedure is called (visited) before its children [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] calls follow preorder. A procedure returns only after all its children return [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns follow postorder.

Answer: S1 is true and S2 is true

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.

S1: Every SLR(1) grammar is unambiguous but there are certain unambiguous grammars that are not SLR(1).
S2: For any context-free grammar, there is a parser that takes at most [latex]O(n^3)[/latex] time to parse a string of length n.

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.B: S1 is false and S2 is true
options.C: S1 is true and S2 is true
options.D: S1 is false and S2 is false

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: an SLR(1) table has no conflicts, so every SLR(1) grammar is unambiguous. Some unambiguous grammars (e.g. many LALR/LR(1) grammars) are not SLR(1) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- S2: the CYK algorithm parses any CFG (in CNF) in [latex]O(n^3)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: S1 is true and S2 is true

questions.question:
Let p and q be two propositions. Consider the following two formulae in propositional logic.

[latex]S1: (\neg p\wedge(p\vee q))\rightarrow q[/latex]
[latex]S2: q\rightarrow(\neg p\wedge(p\vee q))[/latex]

Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are tautologies.
options.B: S1 is a tautology but S2 is not a tautology
options.C: S1 is not a tautology but S2 is a tautology
options.D: Niether S1 nor S2 is a tautology

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: [latex] eg p\wedge(p\vee q)\equiv eg p\wedge q[/latex], and [latex]( eg p\wedge q) ightarrow q[/latex] is always true [latex] ightarrow[/latex] tautology.
- S2: take p = q = 1: q is true but [latex] eg p\wedge(p\vee q)[/latex] is false [latex] ightarrow[/latex] S2 is false [latex] ightarrow[/latex] not a tautology.

Answer: S1 is a tautology but S2 is not a tautology

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements.

S1: Destination MAC address of an ARP reply is a broadcast address.
S2: Destination MAC address of an ARP request is a broadcast address.

Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are true
options.B: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.C: S1 is false and S2 is true
options.D: Both S1 and S2 are false

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- ARP request: the sender does not know the MAC, so it is broadcast [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S2 TRUE.
- ARP reply: sent directly (unicast) to the requester's MAC [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S1 FALSE.

Answer: S1 is false and S2 is true

questions.question:
Consider the following array.

[latex]\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline 23&32&45&69&72&73&89&97 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Which algorithm out of the following options uses the least number of comparisons (among the array elements) to sort the above array in ascending order?

options.A: Selection sort
options.B: Mergesort
options.C: Insertion sort
options.D: Quicksort using the last element as pivot

questions.explanation:
The array is already sorted.
- Insertion sort: each element is compared once with its left neighbour [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] n [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 7 comparisons (best case).
- Selection sort always does n(n [latex]-[/latex] 1)/2 = 28.
- Merge sort needs more than 7 (about 12 here).
- Quicksort with the last element as pivot on sorted input is the worst case (28).

Answer: Insertion sort

questions.question: A binary search tree T contains n distinct elements. What is the time complexity of picking an element in T that is smaller than the maximum element in T?

options.A: [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex]
options.B: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]
options.C: [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex]
options.D: [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Look only at the root and its children:
- If the root has a right child, the root is smaller than something, so it is not the maximum [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] pick the root.
- Otherwise the root is the maximum, and its left child is smaller [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] pick the left child.

A constant number of steps [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex]

questions.question: In the context of operating systems, which of the following statements is/are correct with respect to paging?

options.A: Paging helps solve the issue of external fragmentation
options.B: Page size has no impact on internal fragmentation
options.C: Paging incurs memory overheads
options.D: Multi-level paging is necessary to support pages of different sizes

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Any free frame can hold any page, so there is no external fragmentation [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Larger pages waste more space in the last page (internal fragmentation) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Page tables take memory (and TLB, extra accesses) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Multi-level paging is used to shrink page tables, not to support different page sizes [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 3

questions.question: Let < M > denote an encoding of an automaton M. Suppose that [latex]\Sigma =\{0,1\}[/latex]. Which of the following languages is/are NOT recursive?

options.A: [latex]L= \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a DFA such that } L(M)=\emptyset \}[/latex]
options.B: [latex]L= \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a DFA such that } L(M)=\Sigma ^ * \}[/latex]
options.C: [latex]L= \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a PDA such that } L(M)=\emptyset \}[/latex]
options.D: [latex]L= \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ is a PDA such that } L(M)=\Sigma ^ * \}[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- DFA emptiness: check whether a final state is reachable [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] decidable.
- DFA universality: complement the DFA and check emptiness [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] decidable.
- PDA emptiness: convert to a CFG and check whether S generates any string [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] decidable.
- PDA universality ([latex]L=\Sigma^*[/latex]): undecidable [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not recursive.

Answer: PDA with [latex]L(M)=\Sigma^*[/latex]

questions.question:
Suppose a database system crashes again while recovering from a previous crash. Assume checkpointing is not done by the database either during the transactions or during recovery.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.A: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again
options.B: The system cannot recover any further
options.C: All the transactions that are already undone and redone will not be recovered again
options.D: The database will become inconsistent

questions.explanation:
Without checkpoints, recovery always starts from the log. Undo and redo are idempotent (doing them again gives the same result), so after a second crash the same undo and redo lists are built from the log and applied again.

The database can still recover and stays consistent.

Answer: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again

questions.question: Which of the following standard C library functions will always invoke a system call when executed from a single-threaded process in a UNIX/Linux operating system?

options.A: exit
options.B: malloc
options.C: sleep
options.D: strlen

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- exit: must ask the kernel to end the process [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always a system call.
- sleep: must ask the kernel to suspend the process [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always a system call.
- malloc: often served from already allocated heap memory; calls brk/mmap only sometimes.
- strlen: pure user-space computation.

Answer: exit, sleep

questions.question:
Consider a linear list based directory implementation in a file system. Each directory is a list of nodes, where each node contains the file name along with the file metadata, such as the list of pointers to the data blocks. Consider a given directory foo.

Which of the following operations will necessarily require a full scan of foo for successful completion?

options.A: Creation of a new file in foo
options.B: Deletion of an existing file from foo
options.C: Renaming of an existing file in foo
options.D: Opening of an existing file in foo

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Create: must check that no file with that name already exists [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] scan the whole list.
- Rename: must check that the new name is not already used [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] scan the whole list.
- Delete / open an existing file: stop as soon as the file is found [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not necessarily a full scan.

Answer: Creation of a new file, Renaming of an existing file

questions.question:
There are 6 jobs with distinct difficulty levels, and 3 computers with distinct processing speeds. Each job is assigned to a computer such that:

The fastest computer gets the toughest job and the slowest computer gets the easiest job.
Every computer gets at least one job.

The number of ways in which this can be done is ___________.

The toughest job goes to the fastest and the easiest to the slowest. The other 4 jobs can go to any of the 3 computers: [latex]3^4=81[/latex] ways.

The middle computer must get at least one job; remove the cases where all 4 go to the other two: [latex]2^4=16[/latex].

81 [latex]-[/latex] 16 = 65

Answer: 65

questions.question:
A relation [latex]r(A,B)[/latex] in a relational database has 1200 tuples. The attribute [latex]A[/latex] has integer values ranging from 6 to 20, and the attribute [latex]B[/latex] has integer values ranging from 1 to 20. Assume that the attributes [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are independently distributed.

The estimated number of tuples in the output of [latex]\sigma _{(A > 10)\vee(B=18)}(r)[/latex] is ____________
questions.explanation:
A takes 15 values (6-20) and B takes 20 values (1-20). The official key accepts two answers, depending on what is counted.

Method 1: estimated tuples in the output = 820
- A [latex]\gt[/latex] 10 holds for 11-20, 10 of 15 values [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]P=\frac23[/latex]
- [latex]P(B=18)=\frac1{20}[/latex]
- Independent: [latex]P(A \gt 10\vee B=18)=\frac23+\frac1{20}-\frac23\cdot\frac1{20}=\frac{41}{60}[/latex]
- Estimated tuples [latex]=1200\times\frac{41}{60}=820[/latex]

Method 2: distinct (A, B) value pairs that satisfy the condition = 205
- A [latex]\gt[/latex] 10 with any B: [latex]10\times20=200[/latex] pairs
- B = 18 with A [latex]\le[/latex] 10 (A = 6-10): 5 more pairs
- Total [latex]=200+5=205[/latex]

Answer: 820 (estimated tuples) or 205 (distinct value pairs); both are accepted

questions.question:
Consider the following grammar (that admits a series of declarations, followed by expressions) and the associated syntax directed translation (SDT) actions, given as pseudo-code

[latex]\begin{array}{lll} P & \rightarrow & D^* E^* \\ D & \rightarrow & \textsf{int ID} \{ \text{record that } \textsf{ID.} \text{lexeme is of type} \textsf{ int\}} \\ D & \rightarrow & \textsf{bool ID} \{ \text{record that } \textsf{ID.} \text{lexeme is of type} \textsf{ bool\}} \\ E& \rightarrow & E_1 +E_2 \{ \text{check that } E_1. \text{type}=E_2. \text{type} = \textsf{int}; \text{set } E.\text{type }:= \textsf{int} \} \\ E & \rightarrow & !E_1 \{ \text{check that } E_1. \text{type} = \textsf{bool}; \text{ set } E.\text{type} := \textsf{bool} \} \\ E & \rightarrow & \textsf{ID} \{ \text{set } E. \text{type } := \textsf{int} \} \end{array}[/latex]

With respect to the above grammar, which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: The actions can be used to correctly type-check any syntactically correct program
options.B: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct integer variable declarations and integer expressions
options.C: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct boolean variable declarations and boolean expressions.
options.D: The actions will lead to an infinite loop

questions.explanation:
The rule [latex]E\rightarrow ID[/latex] always sets E.type = int, even when ID was declared bool. So:
- Integer declarations and expressions (+) type-check correctly.
- Boolean expressions fail: !ID would see an int and report an error.
- Nothing loops forever.

Answer: type-check integer variable declarations and integer expressions

questions.question:
The following relation records the age of 500 employees of a company, where empNo ( indicating the employee number) is the key:

[latex]empAge(\underline{empNo},age)[/latex]

Consider the following relational algebra expression:

[latex]\Pi_{empNo}(empAge \Join_{(age > age1)} \rho_{empNo1,age1}(empAge))[/latex]

What does the above expression generate?

options.B: Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is more than the age of exactly one other employee

The join pairs each employee with every employee who is younger (age [latex]\gt[/latex] age1). An employee appears in the result if at least one other employee is younger, i.e. if their age is not the minimum.

questions.question:
Consider the following recurrence relation.
[latex]T\left ( n \right )=\left\{\begin{array} {lcl} T(n/2)+T(2n/5)+7n & \text{if} \; n > 0\\1 & \text{if}\; n=0 \end{array}\right.[/latex]
Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: [latex]T(n)=\Theta (n^{5/2})[/latex]
options.B: [latex]T(n)=\Theta (n \log n)[/latex]
options.C: [latex]T(n)=\Theta (n)[/latex]
options.D: [latex]T(n)=\Theta ((\log n)^{5/2})[/latex]

questions.explanation:
The two subproblems have total size [latex]\frac n2+\frac{2n}{5}=0.9n \lt n[/latex]. The work per level shrinks geometrically: [latex]7n,\ 0.9\cdot7n,\ 0.81\cdot7n,\ldots[/latex]

Total [latex]=7n(1+0.9+0.81+\cdots)=7n\cdot10=\Theta(n)[/latex]

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar where the set of terminals is [latex]\{a,b,c,d,f\}[/latex].

[latex]\begin{array}{lll} S & \rightarrow & d \: a \: T \mid R \: f \\ T & \rightarrow & a \: S \: \mid \: b \: a \: T \: \mid \epsilon \\ R & \rightarrow & c \: a \: T \: R \: \mid \epsilon \end{array}[/latex]

The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table.

Which one of the following choices represents the correct combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table ("blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty)?

options.A: A
options.B: B
options.C: C
options.D: D

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]FIRST(Rf)=\{c,f\}[/latex] (R can be [latex]\epsilon[/latex]) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (1) [S, c] and (2) [S, f] are both [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex].
- [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] goes in FOLLOW(T). T is followed by R in [latex]R\rightarrow caTR[/latex] (gives c, and FOLLOW(R) = {f}), and FOLLOW(T) includes FOLLOW(S) = {$}. So FOLLOW(T) = {c, f, $}.

questions.question:
Let [latex]r_i(z)[/latex] and [latex]w_i(z)[/latex] denote read and write operations respectively on a data item [latex]z[/latex] by a transaction [latex]T_i[/latex]. Consider the following two schedules.

[latex]S1: r_1(x)r_1(y)r_2(x)r_2(y)w_2(y)w_1(x)[/latex]
[latex]S2: r_1(x)r_2(x)r_2(y)w_2(y)r_1(y)w_1(x)[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: S1 is conflict serializable, and S2 is not conflict serializable
options.B: S1 is not conflict serializable, and S2 is conflict serializable
options.C: Both S1 and S2 are conflict serializable
options.D: Niether S1 nor S2 is conflict serializable

questions.explanation:
S1: [latex]r_1(y)[/latex] before [latex]w_2(y)[/latex] gives T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2; [latex]r_2(x)[/latex] before [latex]w_1(x)[/latex] gives T2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1. Cycle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not conflict serializable.

S2: [latex]r_2(x)[/latex] before [latex]w_1(x)[/latex] gives T2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1; [latex]w_2(y)[/latex] before [latex]r_1(y)[/latex] gives T2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1. No cycle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] conflict serializable (T2, T1).

questions.question:
Consider the relation [latex]R(P,Q,S,T,X,Y,Z,W)[/latex] with the following functional dependencies.

[latex]PQ\rightarrow X;\quad P\rightarrow YX;\quad Q\rightarrow Y; \quad Y\rightarrow ZW[/latex]

Consider the decomposition of the relation R into the constituent relations according to the following two decomposition schemes.

[latex]D1:\quad R=[(P,QS,T);\;(P,T,X);\;(Q,Y);\;(Y,Z,W)][/latex]
[latex]D2:\quad R=[(P,Q,S);\;(T,X);\;(Q,Y);\;(Y,Z,W)][/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: D1 is a lossless decomposition, but D2 is a lossy decomposition.
options.B: D1 is a lossy decomposition, but D2 is a lossless decomposition.
options.C: Both D1 and D2 are lossless decompositions.
options.D: Both D1 and D2 are lossy decompositions.

questions.explanation:
D1: join step by step on common attributes that are keys of one side:
- (P, Q, S, T) with (P, T, X) on PT: [latex]P\rightarrow X[/latex] so PT [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] X True
- with (Q, Y) on Q: [latex]Q\rightarrow Y[/latex] True
- with (Y, Z, W) on Y: [latex]Y\rightarrow ZW[/latex] True
So D1 is lossless.

D2: (T, X) shares no attribute with the other relations, so joining it gives a cross product [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] lossy.

Answer: D1 is lossless, but D2 is lossy

questions.question: Let G be a group of order 6, and H be a subgroup of G such that 1 < |H| < 6. Which one of the following options is correct?

options.B: G may not be cyclic, but H is always cyclic.
options.C: G is always cyclic, but H may not be cyclic.
options.D: Both G and H may not be cyclic.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- G can be the non-abelian group [latex]S_3[/latex] (order 6), which is not cyclic.
- By Lagrange, |H| divides 6 and is strictly between 1 and 6, so |H| = 2 or 3, which are primes. Every group of prime order is cyclic.

questions.question:
Consider the two statements.

S2: For all random variables [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex], [latex]\textsf{Cov}[X,Y]=\mathbb E \left[|X-\mathbb E[X]||Y-\mathbb E[Y]|\right ][/latex]

Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are true.
options.B: S1 is true, but S2 is false.
options.C: S1 is false, but S2 is true.
options.D: Both S1 and S2 are false.

Checking each statement:
- S1: the left side is [latex]Cov(X,Y)^2[/latex]. By Cauchy-Schwarz, [latex]Cov(X,Y)^2\le Var(X)Var(Y)[/latex] always, so S1 is FALSE.
- S2: the right side is always [latex]\ge0[/latex], but covariance can be negative (e.g. Y = [latex]-[/latex]X) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] FALSE.

questions.question:
Let [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be an undirected unweighted connected graph. The diameter of [latex]G[/latex] is defined as:
[latex]diam(G)=\displaystyle \max_{u,v \in V} \{ \text{the length of shortest path between }u \text{ and }v \}[/latex]

Let [latex]M[/latex] be the adjacency matrix of [latex]G[/latex].
Define graph [latex]G_2[/latex] on the same set of vertices with adjacency matrix [latex]N[/latex], where

[latex]N_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array} {lcl} 1 &\text{if}\; M_{ij}>0 \text{ or } P_{ij}>0, \text{ where }P=M^2\\0 &\text{otherwise} \end{array}\right.[/latex]

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.A: [latex]diam(G_2)\leq \left \lceil diam(G)/2 \right \rceil[/latex]
options.B: [latex]\left \lceil diam(G)/2 \right \rceil \lt diam(G_2) \lt diam(G)[/latex]
options.C: [latex]diam(G_2) =diam(G)[/latex]
options.D: [latex]diam(G) \lt diam(G_2) \leq 2 \; diam(G)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
[latex]P=M^2[/latex] has [latex]P_{ij} \gt 0[/latex] exactly when there is a path of length 2. So in [latex]G_2[/latex], u and v are adjacent whenever their distance in G is 1 or 2.

A shortest path of length d in G can be covered with [latex]\lceil d/2\rceil[/latex] such jumps, so [latex]diam(G_2)=\lceil diam(G)/2\rceil[/latex].

Answer: [latex]diam(G_2)\le\lceil diam(G)/2\rceil[/latex]

options.B: B

questions.question:
For a Turing machine M, < M > denotes an encoding of M. Consider the following two languages.

[latex]\begin{array}{ll} L1 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ takes more than } 2021 \text{ steps on all inputs} \} \\ L2 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M\text{ takes more than } 2021 \text{ steps on some input} \} \end{array}[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: Both L1 and L2 are decidable.
options.B: L1 is decidable  and L2 is undecidable.
options.C: L1 is undecidable  and L2 is decidable.
options.D: Both L1 and L2 are undecidable.

questions.explanation:
In 2021 steps, M can read at most the first 2021 input symbols. So "more than 2021 steps" depends only on inputs of length up to 2021, a finite set.

Simulate M for 2022 steps on each such input; this decides both "on all inputs" (L1) and "on some input" (L2).

Answer: Both L1 and L2 are decidable

questions.question:
An articulation point in a connected graph is a vertex such that removing the vertex and its incident edges disconnects the graph into two or more connected components.
Let T be a DFS tree obtained by doing DFS in a connected undirected graph G.
Which of the following options is/are correct?

options.A: Root of T can never be an articulation point in G.
options.B: Root of T is an articulation point in G if and only if it has 2 or more children.
options.C: A leaf of T can be an articulation point in G.
options.D: If u is an articulation point in G such that x is an ancestor of u in T and y is a descendent of u in T, then all paths from x to y in G must pass through u.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- The root is an articulation point exactly when it has two or more DFS children: there are no cross edges in an undirected DFS, so its subtrees connect only through the root [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (option 1 is FALSE).
- A leaf of T: removing it leaves the rest of T connected [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] never an articulation point [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Option 4: y's subtree may have a back edge to an ancestor above u (u is an articulation point because of another subtree), giving a path from x to y that avoids u [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Root of T is an articulation point iff it has 2 or more children

Which of the following Boolean expressions is/are equivalent to [latex]\overline F[/latex] (complement of [latex]F[/latex])?

options.B: [latex]X\overline Y + \overline Z[/latex]
options.C: [latex](X+\overline Z)(\overline Y +\overline Z)[/latex]

questions.question:
A relation [latex]R[/latex] is said to be circular if [latex]aRb[/latex] and [latex]bRc[/latex] together imply [latex]cRa[/latex].
Which of the following options is/are correct?

options.A: If a relation S is reflexive and symmetric, then S is an equivalence relation.
options.B: If a relation S is circular and symmetric, then S is an equivalence relation.
options.C: If a relation S is reflexive and circular, then S is an equivalence relation.
options.D: If a relation S is transitive and circular, then S is an equivalence relation.

questions.explanation:
Reflexive + circular gives an equivalence relation:
- Symmetric: aRb and bRb (reflexive) [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] bRa (circular).
- Transitive: aRb and bRc [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] cRa (circular) [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] aRc (symmetric).

The others fail: reflexive + symmetric need not be transitive; circular + symmetric need not be reflexive (e.g. the empty relation); transitive + circular need not be reflexive either.

Answer: Reflexive and circular [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] equivalence relation

questions.question:
Consider a dynamic hashing approach for 4-bit integer keys:

1. There is a main hash table of size 4.
2. The 2 least significant bits of a key is used to index into the main hash table.
3. Initially, the main hash table entries are empty.
4. Thereafter, when more keys are hashed into it, to resolve collisions, the set of all keys corresponding to a main hash table. entry is organized as a binary tree that grows on demand.
5. First, the 3rd least significant bit is used to divide the keys into left and right subtrees.
6. To resolve more collisions, each node of the binary tree is further sub-divided into left and right subtrees based on the 4th least significant bit.

questions.question:
Consider the following instruction sequence where registers [latex]R_1,R_2 \text{ and }R_3[/latex] are general purpose and [latex]MEMORY[X][/latex] denotes the content at the memory location [latex]X[/latex].

[latex]\begin{array}{llc} \textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Semantics} & \textbf{Instruction Size} \text{ (bytes)} \\ \hline \text{MOV } R1, (5000) & R1 \leftarrow \text{MEMORY}[5000] & 4 \\ \hline \text{MOV } R2, (R3) & R2 \leftarrow \text{MEMORY}[R3] & 4 \\ \hline \text{ADD} R2, R1 & R2 \leftarrow R1 + R2 & 2 \\ \hline \text{MOV } (R3), R2 & \text{MEMORY}[R3] \leftarrow R2 & 4 \\ \hline \text{INC } R3 & R3 \leftarrow R3+1 & 2 \\ \hline \text{DEC } R1 & R1 \leftarrow R1-1 & 2 \\ \hline \text{BNZ } 1004 & \text{Branch if not zero to the} & 2 \\ & \text{given absolute address} \\ \hline \text{HALT} & \text{Stop} & 1 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Assume that the content of the memory location 5000 is 10, and the content of the register [latex]R_3[/latex] is 3000. The content of each of the memory locations from 3000 to 3020 is 50. The instruction sequence starts from the memory location 1000. All the numbers are in decimal format. Assume that the memory is byte addressable.
After the execution of the program, the content of memory location 3010 is ____________
questions.explanation:
R1 = MEMORY[5000] = 10, so the loop (BNZ back to 1004) runs 10 times. Each pass adds R1 to MEMORY[R3] and moves R3 one byte ahead.

R3 goes 3000, 3001, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 3009. Location 3010 is never written, so it keeps its value 50.

Answer: 50

questions.question:
The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 7 to 3.

Among the options below, an acceptable value for the total number of students in the class is:
questions.explanation:
Boys : girls = 7 : 3, so the total must be a multiple of 7 + 3 = 10. Only 50 is (35 boys, 15 girls).

Answer: 50

questions.question:
A polygon is convex if, for every pair of points, P and Q belonging to the polygon, the line segment PQ lies completely inside or on the polygon.
Which one of the following is NOT a convex polygon?

options.A: A
options.B: B
options.C: C
options.D: D

questions.explanation:
Shape (A) has a notch (an inward corner). A segment between two points on either side of the notch passes outside the shape, so it is not convex. The triangle, square and trapezium are convex.

Answer: A

questions.question:
Consider the following sentences:

i. Everybody in the class is prepared for the exam.
ii. Babu invited Danish to his home because he enjoys playing chess.

Which of the following is the CORRECT observation about the above two sentences?

options.A: (i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is unambiguous
options.B: (i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is unambiguous
options.C: (i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is ambiguous
options.D: (i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is ambiguous

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- (i) "Everybody ... is prepared" is grammatically correct ("everybody" takes a singular verb).
- (ii) "he" could mean Babu or Danish [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] ambiguous.

Answer: (i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is ambiguous

questions.question: A circular sheet of paper is folded along the lines in the direction shown. The paper, after being punched in the final folded state as shown and unfolded in the reverse order of folding, will look like _______.

options.A: A
options.B: B
options.C: C
options.D: D

questions.explanation:
Unfold in reverse order:
- The punch on the vertical fold line opens into a long horizontal slot at the top; unfolding the horizontal fold copies it to the bottom.
- The small punch on the horizontal fold line opens into a small vertical slot; unfolding the vertical fold copies it to the other side.
- The quarter-circle at the corner becomes a full circle in the centre.

This is pattern (A): long horizontal slots top and bottom, small vertical slots left and right.

Answer: A

questions.question: We have 2 rectangular sheets of paper, M and N, of dimensions 6 cm x 1 cm each. Sheet M is rolled to form an open cylinder by bringing the short edges of the sheet together. Sheet N is cut into equal square patches and assembled to form the largest possible closed cube. Assuming the ends of the cylinder are closed, the ratio of the volume of the cylinder to that of the cube is _________

options.A: [latex]\frac{\pi}{2}[/latex]
options.B: [latex]\frac{3}{\pi}[/latex]
options.C: [latex]\frac{9}{\pi}[/latex]
options.D: [latex]3 \pi [/latex]

questions.explanation:
Cylinder: short edges (1 cm) joined [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] circumference 6, height 1. [latex]r=\frac{3}{\pi}[/latex], [latex]V=\pi r^2h=\frac{9}{\pi}[/latex].

Cube: area 6 cm[latex]^2[/latex] cut into 6 squares of 1 cm[latex]^2[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] side 1, V = 1.

Ratio [latex]=\frac{9}{\pi}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{9}{\pi}[/latex]

questions.question:
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Items} & \textbf{Cost} & \textbf{Profit \%} & \textbf{Marked Price} \\ & (Rs.) & & (Rs.) \\ \hline P &5,400 &---&5,860\\ \hline Q&---&25&10,000\\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Details of prices of two items P and Q are presented in the above table. The ratio of cost of item P to cost of item Q is 3:4. Discount is calculated as the difference between the marked price and the selling price. The profit percentage is calculated as the ratio of the difference between selling price and cost, to the cost
[latex](\text{Profit} \%=\dfrac{\text{Selling price - Cost}}{\text{Cost}} \times 100)[/latex]
The discount on item Q, as a percentage of its marked price, is _______
questions.explanation:
Cost of Q = [latex]5400\times\frac43=7200[/latex].
Selling price of Q = 7200 [latex]\times[/latex] 1.25 = 9000.
Discount = 10000 [latex]-[/latex] 9000 = 1000 = 10% of the marked price.

Answer: 10

questions.question:
There are five bags each containing identical sets of ten distinct chocolates. One chocolate is picked from each bag.
The probability that at least two chocolates are identical is _________
questions.explanation:
P(all 5 different) = [latex]\frac{10\times9\times8\times7\times6}{10^5}=\frac{30240}{100000}=0.3024[/latex]

P(at least two identical) = 1 [latex]-[/latex] 0.3024 = 0.6976

Answer: 0.6976

questions.question:
Given below are two statements 1 and 2, and two conclusions I and II

Statement 1: All bacteria are microorganisms.
Statement 2: All pathogens are microorganisms.

Conclusion I: Some pathogens are bacteria.
Conclusion II: All pathogens are not bacteria.

Based on the above statements and conclusions, which one of the following options is logically CORRECT?

options.A: Only conclusion I is correct
options.B: Only conclusion II is correct
options.C: Either conclusion I or II is correct
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor II is correct

questions.explanation:
Both bacteria and pathogens are inside "microorganisms", but nothing says how bacteria and pathogens relate to each other. They may overlap or not, so neither "some pathogens are bacteria" nor "all pathogens are not bacteria" follows. They are also not complementary (both could fail), so "either" is wrong too.

Answer: Neither conclusion I nor II is correct

questions.question:
Some people suggest anti-obesity measures (AOM) such as displaying calorie information in restaurant menus. Such measures sidestep addressing the core problems that cause obesity: poverty and income inequality.

Which one of the following statements summarizes the passage?

options.A: The proposed AOM addresses the core problems that cause obesity
options.B: If obesity reduces, poverty will naturally reduce, since obesity causes poverty
options.C: AOM are addressing the core problems and are likely to succeed
options.D: AOM are addressing the problem superficially

questions.explanation:
The passage says these measures "sidestep" the core problems (poverty and inequality). So they deal with obesity only on the surface.

Answer: AOM are addressing the problem superficially
